paragraphs: Federated learning requires clients to communicate model updates, and those messages can become expensive. Gradient compression reduces that burden, but the paper questions whether the usual parameter coordinates are the best place to compress. Its central idea is to change the representation of a gradient before applying a compressor.

The proposed mapping uses the structure of input activations and output gradients to produce an alternative space with more near-zero elements. The transformation itself preserves information. This distinction matters: the lossless claim concerns the change of representation, while subsequently discarding small elements can still introduce information loss. A representation with more small entries makes more aggressive sparsification possible with minimal loss.

The authors report stronger compression than the baselines and, in some cases, higher accuracy than uploading full gradients. They also show theoretically that the mapping preserves the existing best-known federated-learning convergence rate through its orthogonal transformation properties. Together, these findings suggest that choosing the coordinates for compression can matter alongside choosing the compressor.
icml-2024-achieving-lossless-gradient-sp.tldr: An information-preserving change of gradient coordinates enables more aggressive communication compression in federated learning with minimal information loss.

paragraphs: Semantic segmentation assigns a category to each image pixel, making reliable annotation labor-intensive. Foundation models and existing crowdsourced datasets offer useful starting labels, but those labels can contain errors. This paper studies how to direct human effort toward correcting them efficiently.

The framework combines two choices: how to ask for a correction and which correction to request next. Instead of asking an annotator to classify a pixel directly, it presents a correction query based on an existing pseudo label. The authors support this design with theoretical analysis and a user study. The selection rule also looks ahead to how a correction can expand through superpixels, which group pixels into regions.

Foundation models supply zero-shot pseudo labels and superpixels for this process. Experiments on PASCAL, Cityscapes, and Kvasir-SEG show improvements over previous active segmentation and label-correction methods. The authors also use the framework to revise PASCAL, correcting errors across 2.6 million pixels. The contribution therefore concerns both making annotation interactions easier and selecting interactions with broader corrective value.
icml-2024-active-label-correction-for-se.tldr: A foundation-model-assisted annotation framework improves semantic segmentation label correction through easier queries and superpixel-aware selection.

paragraphs: A generated image collection can look diverse while misrepresenting how often particular attributes appear. This paper proposes evaluating those mismatches explicitly, comparing the distribution of attribute strengths in generated images with the training set. The goal is to explain what a generator overproduces or underproduces.

Single-attribute Divergence measures mismatches for individual attributes. Paired-attribute Divergence compares joint distributions, allowing it to expose incorrect relationships between attributes even when individual frequencies are less revealing. To measure attribute strength, the authors introduce Heterogeneous CLIPScore, which uses cosine similarity between image and text vectors with heterogeneous initial points.

The resulting analysis identifies implausible combinations such as babies with beards in ProjectedGAN despite competitive conventional scores. It also finds that diffusion models struggle with color diversity and that larger sampling timesteps in the studied latent diffusion model produce more small objects such as jewelry. In their evaluation, Stable Diffusion v1.5 captures attributes better than v2.1. These findings illustrate how interpretable distribution comparisons can reveal specific weaknesses hidden by broad quality or diversity scores.
icml-2024-attribute-based-interpretable-.tldr: Attribute-level distribution metrics reveal which visual traits and trait combinations generative models misrepresent.

paragraphs: When an AI system chooses an action under uncertainty, it can compare the expected outcomes of its alternatives. Those expectations depend on probabilities. This paper examines a foundational question behind that process: when can a machine learn probabilities that describe objective facts about its environment?

The authors frame probabilities as properties of the environment that a model aims to represent. Under this interpretation, learning a probability function is a claim about recovering something objectively true. The qualification that such probabilities exist is part of the question itself. Their existence and a machine’s ability to learn them are therefore separate issues that the paper brings into focus.

The contribution is theoretical: under basic assumptions, the authors prove results identifying when true objective probabilities can be learned and when they cannot. These positive and negative results place conditions around the probabilistic learning that supports decisions based on expected outcomes. The stated conclusion is conditional, rather than a blanket assertion that machines can always recover environmental probabilities or that such recovery is impossible.
icml-2024-can-machines-learn-the-true-pr.tldr: The paper proves conditional results about when machines can and cannot learn true objective probabilities.

paragraphs: Transferring knowledge between tables is difficult because their entries and columns may not line up. The same entity can have different names, and columns can differ in naming, order, or availability. CARTE addresses this integration problem with a neural architecture that does not require those correspondences to be established first.

The method represents tabular or relational data as a graph. String embeddings represent both entries and column names, allowing an open vocabulary. A graph-attention network then interprets entries using their column names and neighboring entries. This contextual representation allows the model to process tables with different columns and to pretrain on background data that has not been matched.

An extensive benchmark finds that CARTE outperforms a strong collection of baselines, including leading tree-based models. The architecture also supports joint learning across tables with unmatched columns, allowing larger tables to help learning on a smaller one. The broader significance is a practical route toward pretrained tabular models that reduces the need for explicit data alignment before knowledge can be shared.
icml-2024-carte-pretraining-and-transfer.tldr: CARTE enables pretraining and transfer across tables without first matching their entities or columns.

paragraphs: Clients in federated learning can have substantially different data, making a single shared model a poor fit. Clustered federated learning addresses this by grouping clients and learning a model for each group. The challenge is identifying useful groups when clients do not directly share their local datasets.

This paper proposes using similarities in model updates as the basis for grouping. The algorithm periodically accumulates and clusters gradients that clients compute for various models. These gradients provide information about how clients respond to the models, allowing the grouping process to operate within the stated federated setting without direct access to their datasets.

The authors analyze the resulting learning procedure and establish a near-optimal error rate for stochastic convergence to optimal models under mild conditions. They also evaluate it on several clustered federated-learning benchmarks, reporting improvements in convergence speed, clustering accuracy, and task performance. The combined message is that gradient-based grouping can improve both the identification of client groups and the models trained for those groups.
icml-2024-clustered-federated-learning-v.tldr: Clustering accumulated client gradients improves federated client grouping and learning, with a conditional near-optimal convergence guarantee.

paragraphs: Evaluating an AI system becomes difficult when the system knows more than its evaluator. This paper studies an analogous situation: stronger language models receive information needed to answer a question, while weaker evaluators lack that information. It asks whether a structured exchange between informed models can help the less-informed evaluator identify the correct answer.

The tested protocol is debate. Two expert models argue for different answers, and a non-expert chooses between them. Debate improves accuracy for both model and human evaluators in the experiments. Non-expert models reach 76% accuracy compared with 48% for naive baselines; humans reach 88% compared with 60%. These results show that the arguments can make useful information accessible to the evaluator.

The authors also optimize the expert debaters for persuasiveness without supervised training, finding that this further improves evaluators’ ability to identify the truth. The result is encouraging empirical evidence for debate as an alignment method when ground truth is unavailable. Its force comes from the tested information-asymmetry setting, rather than a universal guarantee about persuasive arguments.
icml-2024-debating-with-more-persuasive-.tldr: In an information-asymmetry experiment, debate helps weaker evaluators find correct answers, and training more persuasive debaters improves that ability.

paragraphs: Some learning objectives combine a finite collection of terms, each containing an expectation that cannot be computed directly. Training then involves two kinds of sampling: selecting terms and estimating their expectations. This paper analyzes stochastic gradient descent when both sources of randomness are present, a setting relevant to diffusion models and variational autoencoders.

The authors establish convergence results for independent minibatching and random reshuffling under general conditions. Their framework also permits dependence between the gradient estimators for different components. That matters because correlations can affect optimization behavior, and the analysis makes it possible to examine their effects in finer detail.

The theory also addresses how to distribute a fixed per-iteration computation budget. With minibatch size b and m Monte Carlo samples, the budget scales as b times m; the analysis provides guidance about where additional effort should go. Finally, the authors prove that random reshuffling improves the complexity dependence on subsampling noise. The contribution connects convergence theory to concrete choices about sampling and computational allocation.
icml-2024-demystifying-sgd-with-doubly-s.tldr: A convergence analysis of doubly stochastic SGD clarifies correlation effects, computation allocation, and the benefits of random reshuffling.

paragraphs: Minimax optimization involves one participant minimizing an objective while another maximizes it. In nonconvex-nonconcave problems, using different update timescales can help algorithms find local minimax points. Existing methods, however, can struggle at non-strict local minimax points, which the paper identifies as common in overparameterized settings.

The authors isolate two problems. Some existing methods remain unstable at certain non-strict points even when the timescale separation is sufficiently large. Separately, calculating an appropriate separation can be impractical. The paper introduces two modifications to two-timescale extragradient methods: a double-step alternating update and a scheme that increases the timescale separation.

Under mild conditions, the proposed methods converge to non-strict local minimax points that the existing two-timescale methods fail to reach. This is a targeted improvement in the class of local solutions that the methods can handle. The result addresses both update stability and the difficulty of choosing a suitable timescale separation, while retaining the conditional nature of the convergence guarantees.
icml-2024-double-step-alternating-extrag.tldr: Two modifications to extragradient methods enable conditional convergence to non-strict local minimax points that existing two-timescale methods cannot reach.

paragraphs: Electron density is a spatial function central to understanding chemical systems and to density functional theory simulations. Predicting it requires representing variation across space, including both broad patterns and finer detail. This paper introduces a neural operator designed around that functional character of the prediction task.

The Gaussian plane-wave neural operator combines plane-wave and Gaussian-type orbital bases, both familiar in density functional theory. These bases supply complementary ways to represent the density. Their combination allows the method to capture both high-frequency and low-frequency components effectively. The architecture operates in an infinite-dimensional function space, making the representation of the target function a central design choice.

The authors evaluate GPWNO on QM9, MD, and Material Project datasets and report superior performance over ten baselines. The stated findings support combining complementary representations for electron-density prediction across the tested datasets. The approach matters because it connects the model’s representation directly to the different spatial scales present in the quantity being estimated, rather than treating all density variation as a single undifferentiated prediction problem.
icml-2024-gaussian-plane-wave-neural-ope.tldr: GPWNO combines Gaussian and plane-wave representations to predict electron density across spatial scales, outperforming ten baselines in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Weather, climate, and cosmic microwave background data are naturally represented on a sphere. Neural models that predict a signal directly from coordinates can struggle to preserve the intricate details of highly nonlinear spherical signals. This paper develops a hybrid representation to address that difficulty.

HNeR-S uses spherical feature grids to obtain positional features, then combines those features with a multilayer perceptron to predict the signal. The grid supplies a spatially organized representation that works alongside the neural network. The authors consider equirectangular grids for weather data and hierarchical equal-area isolatitude pixelization grids for cosmic microwave background data, aligning the representation with each data setting.

The method is evaluated on regression, super-resolution, temporal interpolation, and compression. These tasks examine whether the representation can fit signals, recover finer spatial detail, estimate intermediate times, and store information compactly. The authors report extensive evidence of its effectiveness across these uses. The contribution is a shared hybrid modeling approach that accommodates spherical data while combining structured spatial features with neural prediction.
icml-2024-hybrid-neural-representations-.tldr: HNeR-S combines spherical feature grids with a neural network to represent detailed weather, climate, and cosmic microwave background signals.

paragraphs: A dataset can contain several misleading correlations that a model uses as shortcuts. Removing reliance on one shortcut can increase reliance on another, so addressing biases independently may create competing training pressures. This paper treats those conflicts as a multi-objective optimization problem.

The proposed method first divides training data into groups that induce different shortcuts. It then trains on a weighted combination of the groups’ losses, dynamically adjusting the weights to reduce conflicts in performance. The optimization is designed to encourage a minimax Pareto solution, balancing the competing group objectives with attention to the worst-performing objective. The abstract describes this as an encouraged outcome rather than an unconditional guarantee.

The authors also introduce MultiCelebA, a benchmark intended to test methods under challenging combinations of biases. Their method achieves the best reported performance on three datasets containing multiple biases and also performs strongly on conventional single-bias datasets. These results support coordinating bias mitigation across groups instead of assuming that improvements against separate shortcuts will automatically reinforce one another.
icml-2024-improving-robustness-to-multip.tldr: Dynamically balancing group losses helps models address multiple shortcut correlations whose mitigation can otherwise conflict.

paragraphs: Pretraining can help reinforcement-learning agents interpret visual observations, but success in familiar environments does not establish that the learned representation transfers elsewhere. This paper investigates which pretraining objectives support generalization, addressing earlier evaluations that used different setups or focused mainly on environments resembling the training data.

The authors introduce Atari-PB, a benchmark that pretrains a ResNet-50 on 10 million transitions from 50 Atari games. They then evaluate across diverse environment distributions. This shared experimental framework allows them to compare objectives according to whether their benefits persist as the evaluation environment changes.

The experiments find that objectives emphasizing task-agnostic features, such as recognizing objects and understanding temporal dynamics, improve generalization across environments. Objectives emphasizing task-specific knowledge, such as identifying agents or fitting reward functions, help in similar environments but not varied ones. The distinction matters for choosing what pretraining should teach: knowledge useful for the original tasks can have a different transfer profile from more broadly applicable visual and temporal features.
icml-2024-investigating-pre-training-obj.tldr: Atari-PB finds that task-agnostic pretraining objectives generalize across environments better than objectives focused on task-specific knowledge.

paragraphs: Reducing a convolutional network’s depth can improve inference speed while preserving predictive performance. A common strategy removes activation functions so that consecutive convolution layers can be merged. However, merging enlarges convolution kernels, which can consume much of the latency benefit obtained from having fewer layers.

LayerMerge addresses this tradeoff by choosing convolution layers and activation layers for removal together. Its objective is to reach a desired inference speedup while minimizing performance loss. Coordinating these choices allows the method to account for the cost of the resulting merged layers, rather than treating depth reduction alone as the goal.

The possible removal combinations form an exponentially large search space. The authors therefore construct a surrogate optimization problem and solve it efficiently with dynamic programming. Across the tested architectures, LayerMerge consistently outperforms existing depth-compression and layer-pruning approaches on image classification and generation tasks. The results support making pruning and merging decisions jointly when the practical objective is faster inference with limited loss of model performance.
icml-2024-layermerge-neural-network-dept.tldr: LayerMerge jointly prunes convolution and activation layers to reduce network depth without losing speed gains to oversized merged kernels.

paragraphs: Bayesian neural networks require inference over distributions of model parameters. Those distributions can have many high-density regions in a high-dimensional space, making them difficult to explore. Stochastic gradient MCMC with cyclical learning rates is promising, but reaching different regions can require many sampling steps.

This paper proposes meta-learning an SGMCMC strategy that explores multimodal target distributions more efficiently. The learned procedure is designed to move quickly through high-density regions of the posterior landscape. Learning how to explore addresses the cost of obtaining useful samples, rather than relying only on a prescribed learning-rate schedule.

The authors show that the learned exploration behavior transfers across tasks, including tasks absent from meta-training. Experiments on image classification benchmarks and other downstream tasks report substantially improved sampling efficiency and better performance than vanilla SGMCMC, without significant computational overhead. These findings suggest that exploration behavior learned during meta-training can remain useful beyond its original tasks and reduce the sampling burden of Bayesian neural-network inference in the evaluated settings.
icml-2024-learning-to-explore-for-stocha.tldr: A meta-learned SGMCMC strategy explores multimodal posteriors more efficiently and transfers that exploration behavior to unseen tasks.

paragraphs: GFlowNets generate compositional structures through sequences of probabilistic choices. Temperature-conditioned versions let users control the balance between exploring different possibilities and concentrating on rewarding ones. Training a single model across temperatures is challenging because different temperatures can produce very different gradients and policy-score magnitudes.

Logit-GFN addresses this numerical problem through its architecture. It learns a function of temperature that directly scales the policy’s logits, the scores used to determine its choices. The authors find that this change substantially reduces the training difficulty and greatly accelerates training of temperature-conditioned GFlowNets.

The benefits extend to two learning settings in the reported biological and chemical tasks. In offline learning, Logit-GFN improves generalization from available data. In online learning, it improves the discovery of modes, or distinct promising regions of the target distribution. The results support treating the way temperature enters the model as an important architectural decision: direct learned scaling can make temperature control easier to train while improving the resulting generative behavior.
icml-2024-learning-to-scale-logits-for-t.tldr: Learning to scale policy logits by temperature accelerates GFlowNet training and improves reported generalization and mode discovery.

paragraphs: Unsupervised outlier detection starts with data containing both ordinary examples and outliers, without labels identifying either group. Fully trained likelihood-based deep generative models often struggle to distinguish them. This paper argues that likelihood can nevertheless be useful when the model is deliberately kept under-fitted.

The method rests on an observed inlier-memorization effect: early in training, the generative model memorizes inliers before outliers. ODIM uses this early training behavior to identify inliers and filter outliers. The timing is central to the approach because the useful separation appears before the model has fully fitted the mixed training data.

ODIM requires only a few updates, and the authors report that it is at least tens of times faster than other deep-learning-based algorithms. They evaluate it on close to 60 datasets spanning tables, images, and text, reporting strong detection performance across these data types. The findings show how an intermediate stage of generative-model training can provide a useful detection signal that is often ineffective after full training.
icml-2024-odim-outlier-detection-via-lik.tldr: ODIM detects outliers using the early training period when generative models memorize inliers first, requiring only a few updates.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates how a target policy would perform using data collected by another policy. Standard approaches typically require overlap: the historical policy must provide coverage relevant to the target policy. Without that coverage, some contributions to the target policy’s value cannot be directly established from the observations.

This paper replaces a fully specified outcome model with nonparametric assumptions, especially Lipschitz smoothness, which limits how quickly expected outcomes can change. Under these assumptions, the authors derive sharp upper and lower bounds on policy value. Sharpness means the bounds capture the remaining uncertainty permitted by the assumptions, avoiding unnecessary conservatism.

For Lipschitz smoothness, two linear programs bound the contribution from the region without overlap. The authors derive concise closed-form solutions and prove convergence to the sharp bounds at a minimax-optimal rate up to logarithmic factors. Two semi-synthetic examples yield informative, valid bounds tighter than those available without smoothness. The result offers principled partial identification when the data cannot support a single fully identified policy-value estimate.
icml-2024-off-policy-evaluation-beyond-o.tldr: Smoothness assumptions enable sharp, efficiently estimated bounds on policy value even where historical data lack overlap.

paragraphs: Scene graph generation represents objects in an image and the relationships between them as a graph. Message-passing neural networks update object features using surrounding objects, but the paper identifies two gaps: insufficient use of object co-occurrence and an imbalanced training distribution with many rare cases.

The proposed strategy addresses these issues with two components. CooK incorporates knowledge about which objects occur together. A learnable term frequency–inverse document frequency mechanism, called TF-l-IDF, targets the long-tail distribution. This adds a frequency-based mechanism to approaches that previously addressed imbalance through sampling and learning methods.

On the scene graph generation benchmark, the authors report improvements of up to 3.8% over existing state-of-the-art models for the SGGen subtask. They also observe consistent improvements across the message-passing models evaluated, supporting the strategy’s applicability across those architectures. The findings suggest that explicitly representing co-occurrence and accounting for uneven frequencies can complement the neighborhood information already exchanged by message-passing networks.
icml-2024-scene-graph-generation-strateg.tldr: Object co-occurrence knowledge and learnable frequency weighting improve scene graph generation across the evaluated message-passing models.

paragraphs: Large language models are expensive to deploy, and this paper identifies memory bandwidth as the main bottleneck for single-batch generative inference. Reducing weight precision can ease that bottleneck, but quantization can degrade model quality. SqueezeLLM is a post-training framework designed to improve the tradeoff between memory use and performance.

The framework combines sensitivity-based non-uniform quantization with a dense-and-sparse decomposition. Second-order information guides precision assignment according to weight sensitivity. Outliers and sensitive values are stored separately in an efficient sparse format. Together, these choices allow the compressed representation to account for weights whose quantization requires particular care.

The authors describe lossless compression down to 3-bit precision and report improved quantization performance at the same memory budget. On LLaMA models, 3-bit SqueezeLLM reduces the perplexity gap from FP16 by up to a factor of 2.1 compared with competing methods using the same memory. Deployment on an A6000 GPU yields up to 2.3 times speedup over the baseline. These reported results connect compression quality with practical inference efficiency.
icml-2024-squeezellm-dense-and-sparse-qu.tldr: SqueezeLLM combines sensitivity-aware quantization with sparse storage of exceptional weights to improve low-bit model quality and inference speed.

paragraphs: Deep reinforcement learning can solve combinatorial optimization problems, but learning often requires many reward evaluations. That becomes costly when assessing a candidate solution is computationally intensive. Symmetric replay training aims to extract more training value from high-reward samples that have already been discovered.

The method uses symmetric trajectories associated with those successful samples. During replay, the policy is trained to increase the likelihood of these trajectories, encouraging exploration of symmetric regions that have received less attention. This process does not require additional online interactions. The claimed free exploration refers to that interaction saving, while the method still performs replay training.

SRT is designed as a simple addition that can be integrated into different deep reinforcement-learning methods. Experiments report consistent sample-efficiency improvements across diverse methods on tasks including molecular optimization and hardware design. The findings support using symmetry to extend the usefulness of existing successful experience, particularly when obtaining another reward evaluation is a major part of the cost of learning.
icml-2024-symmetric-replay-training-enha.tldr: Symmetric replay training reuses successful trajectories to improve exploration and sample efficiency without additional online interactions.

paragraphs: Multi-plane representations make neural radiance fields fast to train and query by projecting onto learned grids and interpolating features. However, the paper finds that their preference for fine detail can make broad, low-frequency structure inefficient to represent. With sparse training poses, this can lead to unstable learning and wasted parameters.

The proposed method pairs the multi-plane representation with a coordinate-based multilayer perceptron, whose bias favors low-frequency signals. The coordinate network captures broad structure, while the grid representation focuses on finer detail. Residual connections preserve the characteristic behavior of each component, and a progressive training scheme accelerates the separation of their roles.

Experiments on both static and dynamic neural radiance fields with sparse inputs show improvements over baseline models. The method also achieves comparable results with fewer parameters. These findings support allocating different kinds of scene structure to representations suited to learning them, rather than asking the multi-plane component to spend substantial capacity on both broad patterns and fine details.
icml-2024-synergistic-integration-of-coo.tldr: Combining a coordinate network for broad structure with multi-plane features for fine detail improves sparse-input neural radiance fields.

paragraphs: Stepwise inference methods, including scratchpads and chain-of-thought, help language models tackle problems through intermediate steps. This paper introduces a synthetic graph-navigation task to study how that behavior arises. An autoregressive Transformer must traverse a path from a starting node to a goal, giving researchers a controlled setting with an explicitly multistep structure.

Within this setting, the authors reproduce several phenomena associated with larger models. They trace the observed stepwise reasoning gap to the structure of the training data and examine how changing sampling temperature trades accuracy against output diversity. They also identify a preference for simpler outputs.

The study additionally observes compositional generalization and a primacy bias when examples are supplied in context, meaning that earlier exemplars receive preferential influence. These findings make the synthetic task useful for examining multiple aspects of stepwise inference within one framework. The paper offers mechanistic hypotheses grounded in that setting, providing a basis for further understanding rather than claiming a complete explanation of reasoning in large language models.
icml-2024-towards-an-understanding-of-st.tldr: A synthetic graph-navigation task reproduces several stepwise-inference phenomena and supports mechanistic hypotheses about Transformer behavior.

paragraphs: Hyperparameter tuning becomes expensive as learning problems grow. This paper formalizes a tuning-free algorithm as one that uses only loose hints about problem parameters yet matches an optimally tuned algorithm up to polylogarithmic factors. It focuses on when that standard can be achieved relative to stochastic gradient descent.

For bounded optimization domains, the authors show that matching tuned SGD is possible and that several existing algorithms already do so. For convex smooth or Lipschitz objectives on unbounded domains, they prove a general impossibility result. Additional conditions can change that conclusion: DoG and DoWG qualify as tuning-free when the noise distribution is sufficiently well behaved.

For finding stationary points of smooth, possibly nonconvex functions, the paper gives an SGD variant that matches the best-known high-probability rate of tuned SGD with only a polylogarithmic extra cost. A separate impossibility result rules out matching tuned SGD’s optimal expected rate with high probability. This distinction matters because an average-performance guarantee and a guarantee that holds with high probability impose different requirements.
icml-2024-tuning-free-stochastic-optimiz.tldr: The paper establishes when tuning-free optimization can match tuned SGD and proves limits tied to domain, noise, and guarantee type.

paragraphs: Group-equivariant convolutional networks build in structured responses to transformations such as rotations or color shifts. Real data may support only some of those transformations, and the appropriate degree of symmetry can vary between examples. A fixed symmetry group, or a single fixed restriction of it, cannot fully express that variation.

VP G-CNN makes partial equivariance depend on the input. It conditions the distribution of output group elements on each data instance, allowing different examples to receive different levels of equivariance. Variational inference is used to avoid overfitting. The authors also redesign the reparameterizable distribution to address training instability in models with discrete group equivariance.

Experiments cover toy and real-world datasets, including MNIST67-180, CIFAR10, ColorMNIST, and Flowers102. The authors report robust performance, including on uncertainty metrics. The contribution is an adaptive treatment of symmetry: the model can learn how much rotational or color-shift structure is appropriate for an individual input instead of applying the same equivariance level throughout the dataset.
icml-2024-variational-partial-group-conv.tldr: VP G-CNN learns input-specific levels of rotation and color-shift equivariance using a variational approach.
